extracted.intended_audience: Power-sector stakeholders, regulated entities, state permitting authorities, and other participants in EPA NSPS rulemaking for combustion turbines (e.g., utility developers, environmental consultants, regulators, commenters).
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rationale used by EPA to determine the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for new base-load combined cycle combustion turbines, including cost analyses, technological feasibility (CCS at 90% capture), non-air impacts, and compliance timing. Applies to setting phased standards of performance and compliance dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of CCS cost trends and learning effects
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA expects that as CCS infrastructure increases, technologies will become more economically competitive; planned large-scale projects, pilot plants, and research initiatives will decrease capital and operating costs. Learning rates from analogous energy technologies (5–27%) and historical studies showing capture costs falling (e.g., ~50% fall by 2025 vs 2010) inform cost projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historic learning curves and evidence from analogous technologies, public project tracking (e.g., Global CCS Institute), and studies to project future cost declines and incorporate those trends into assessments of cost-reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NETL Quality Guidelines / CO2 Transport Cost Model
rubrics_metrics.description: NETL's 'Quality Guidelines for Energy System Studies; Carbon Dioxide Transport and Sequestration Costs in NETL Studies' provides estimation of CO2 transport costs based on the CO2 Transport Cost Model, estimating pipeline capital, related capital expenditures, and O&M costs for a single point-to-point pipeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate transport costs using the NETL model inputs and methods; include pipeline capital and O&M components and reflect single point-to-point pipeline assumptions where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequestration cost components per NETL guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequestration costs reflect site screening and evaluation, permitting and construction costs, injection wells and equipment, O&M, pore volume acquisition expense, and long-term liability protection; permitting/construction costs should reflect UIC Class VI and GHGRP subpart RR requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model sequestration costs by including all listed elements and by geographic/generic plant location assumptions (e.g., Midwest, Texas, North Dakota, Montana) as done in NETL energy system studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary sequestration project cost drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary cost drivers are the rate of injection into the reservoir and the areal extent of the CO2 plume; these depend on reservoir thickness, permeability, and sequestration capacity (sequestration coefficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reservoir characteristics (thickness, permeability, sequestration coefficient) to estimate injection well counts, injection rates, plume extent, and resulting testing/monitoring costs; NETL models cumulative storage potential accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of IIJA and IRA investments in cost assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions in the IIJA and IRA (e.g., Carbon Dioxide Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation program, Regional Direct Air Capture Hubs, CarbonSAFE) are expected to increase CO2 pipeline infrastructure and sequestration site development, reducing CCS costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for federal infrastructure and program funding that could reduce transport and sequestration costs when evaluating CCS cost-reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of IRC section 45Q tax credit in CCS cost calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA takes into account the IRC section 45Q tax credit (as revised by the IRA), available at $85/metric ton, which offsets a significant portion of capture, transport, and sequestration costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model capture/transport/sequestration economics both with and without 45Q revenue; treat the credit as a material revenue stream during its statutory availability period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amortization over expected operating life with tax-credit temporality
rubrics_metrics.description: In NSPS analysis, costs are amortized over expected operating life (e.g., 30 years for a new combustion turbine) but adjusted to reflect that the 45Q tax credit is only available for 12 years; EPA modeled higher capacity factors and revenues during the 12-year credit period and lower capacity factors thereafter to keep the 30-year average consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a revenue (like 45Q) is time-limited, model differing capacity factors, revenues, and operating decisions during the credit period vs post-credit period and amortize capital over full useful life while reflecting temporal revenue asymmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario-based cost calculations (operate vs. not operate capture post-credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA calculated two CCS cost sets: one assuming continued operation of capture equipment after the tax credit expires, and one assuming the capture system is not operated during the later period; these yield different $/MWh and $/ton metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate multiple operational scenarios (continued capture vs. shutdown of capture after incentive expiration) to capture the range of plausible compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative and sensitivity cost adjustments (e.g., 5% reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered its CCS cost estimates to be conservatively high (not accounting for some efficiency measures or tech advances) and therefore also calculated costs with an assumed 5% reduction to approximate likely improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform sensitivity analyses applying plausible percentage cost reductions to account for efficiency gains, exhaust gas recirculation, and other feasible improvements; report both conservative and adjusted estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of potential CO2 revenue streams beyond tax credit period
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA acknowledged potential revenues after the 12-year tax credit (e.g., sale of CO2 for utilization, state or corporate credits) that could reduce net compliance costs, but conservatively did not assume such revenues in base estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document potential post-incentive revenue sources but, unless reliably quantifiable, treat them separately from conservative base-case cost estimates; consider scenario runs including such revenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity factor assumptions and sensitivity (80%/31% illustrative case and 60–80% constant cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used illustrative capacity factor scenarios (e.g., 80% for initial 12 years and 31% for remaining 18 years yielding a 30-year average of 51%) and also evaluated constant 60–80% scenarios amortized over 30 years to test cost-reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model and report costs under a range of credible capacity factors consistent with dispatch expectations and market/regulatory drivers; justify chosen primary policy case and show alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of CCS costs to other control costs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA compared CCS costs for representative new base load turbines to costs of other controls in prior EPA rules for fossil fuel-fired EGUs and for other greenhouse gas controls and found CCS costs generally lower, supporting reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark CCS compliance costs against historical EPA control-cost metrics and other GHG control costs to assess cost-reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy requirements and parasitic load impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: A 90%+ carbon capture system increases parasitic/auxiliary energy demand and reduces net power output (e.g., de-rating by 11% for a 500 MWe-net plant), though projects can scale larger to meet net output targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify parasitic loads and net output impacts, consider options to scale gross capacity to deliver specified net output, and assess implications for dispatch and plant design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-GHG air pollutant emissions considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Installation/operation of CCS itself does not impact a unit's potential-to-emit criteria air pollutants; scaling larger could increase non-GHG emissions, but most pollutants would be mitigated by equipment needed to meet other CAA requirements (e.g., low-NOx burners, SCR, FGD generally not necessary for natural gas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether CCS deployment will change PTEs and ensure that BACT/LAER/MACT and other permitting requirements are applied to mitigate any increases; quantify likely pollutant changes and control strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific mitigation for amine solvent degradation products
rubrics_metrics.description: For some amine solvents, NOx can form nitrosamines in the absorber; a conventional multistage water wash or acid wash and a mist eliminator at CO2 scrubber exit is effective at removing gaseous amine and degradation products (e.g., nitrosamine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify and require appropriate solvent emission control measures (e.g., multistage water/acid wash, demister) and material/operational safeguards (compatible materials, interstage cooling) to limit nitrosamine, acetaldehyde, and formaldehyde formation and emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water use impacts and cooling requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS increases cooling water requirements for a combined cycle EGU (NETL: from 190 gallons/MWh without CCS to 290 gallons/MWh with CCS — ~50% increase), though absolute amounts remain small relative to coal-fired EGUs; dry or hybrid cooling for capture can reduce additional water need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify incremental water needs, compare to regional availability and industry precedent, and evaluate use of dry/hybrid cooling to mitigate impacts where water is constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community impacts and meaningful engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA recognizes concerns about disproportionate burdens on historically disadvantaged and overburdened communities and expects meaningful engagement requirements and public permitting processes to provide opportunities for affected stakeholders to raise concerns and for permitting authorities/developers to consider protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement robust, early, and meaningful community engagement processes as described in the preamble (and section X.E.1.b.i), ensure public notice/comment in permitting, and use permitting review to address localized impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing regulatory frameworks to limit localized harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects will be subject to major NSR requirements (BACT, LAER, offsets), PHMSA oversight of supercritical CO2 pipeline safety, UIC Class VI under SDWA, and GHGRP reporting to protect USDWs and ensure sequestration security; MACT/section 112(g) may apply for HAPs on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate CCS permitting and design with existing federal/state regulatory programs (NSR, PHMSA, UIC Class VI, GHGRP, CAA section 112) to ensure comprehensive protection and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability assessment and alternative compliance options
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA concluded CCS as BSER will not cause reliability concerns because CCS costs are reasonable, companies have alternative generation options (intermediate/low-load turbines, renewables, storage), and co-firing low-GHG hydrogen is an allowed compliance alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider grid reliability implications, availability of alternative generation pathways, and whether compliance choices provide sufficient options to avoid undue reliability risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of extent of CO2 reductions and heat-rate impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Designating CCS at 90% capture avoids large CO2 quantities over 30 years (e.g., nearly 41 million tons avoided for a base-load combined cycle EGU) but 90% capture does not equate to 90% emissions reduction due to parasitic energy — NETL baseline: gross heat rate +7%, net heat rate +13%, gross/net emissions reduced by 89.3% and 88.7% respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both capture percentages and net emissions reductions accounting for parasitic energy/heat-rate impacts; quantify lifetime avoided emissions and present gross vs net reduction metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of technological development as a factor in BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered whether adopting CCS as BSER will promote CCS development and concluded it would—by combining standards with 45Q and infrastructure investments, a CCS-based standard incentivizes better solvents, capture components, and experience on lower-CO2-concentration sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether regulation will incentivize broader technology improvement and deployment, including spillover benefits to other industrial sources and retrofit potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER structure: two components and phased standards
rubrics_metrics.description: BSER for base-load turbines contains two components: (1) most efficient generation (phase 1 standard reflecting best-performing combustion turbine systems, effective immediately), and (2) CCS at 90% capture (phase 2 standard reflecting implementation of 90% capture on highly efficient combined cycle systems; compliance date Jan 1, 2032).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining BSER, explicitly specify component technologies, phase-in approaches, phase-specific standards, and effective/compliance dates; provide clear delineation of immediate vs later obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting compliance dates and extension mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalized a January 1, 2032 compliance date for phase 2 (earlier than proposed 2035) after considering comments and information; a compliance date extension of up to 1 year is available where delays in installation/startup of controls are beyond owner/operator control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set compliance dates based on project timelines, stakeholder input, and available capacity for design/construct/operate; include narrowly defined extension mechanisms for circumstances beyond control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project timeline assumptions for CCS deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA bases timelines on Sargent & Lundy capture plant schedules (baseline ~6.25 years; extended ~7 years) and notes differences for new combustion turbines (ability to begin substantial work earlier because state plan requirements are not required), but ultimately used a 7-year planning assumption for new sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established project schedule baselines (e.g., FEED, permitting, right-of-way, construction) to set feasible compliance lead-times; account for whether state-plan processes apply to affected source types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated and deployable-at-scale requirement for BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111, to qualify as BSER, a control technology must be 'adequately demonstrated' for affected sources and the EPA must show industry can deploy it at scale within the compliance timeframe; adequate demonstration does not require that the technology already be in widespread commercial use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document demonstrations, commercial-scale examples, engineering studies, and deployment capacity to show adequate demonstration and scale-up feasibility; respond to comments asserting widespread use is required with statutory interpretation and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple modeling and evidence sources for cost and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relied on multiple sources (EIA AEO, NREL ATB, NETL studies, DOE case studies, IPM model projections, Global CCS Institute data) to estimate costs, learning, capacity factors, and deployment feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangulate cost and feasibility estimates using diverse authoritative sources and modeling tools; document assumptions and reconcile differences across sources.
